title: From kubectl apply to a running container
subtitle: One Deployment, nine components, no magic
scenario:
You have a `deployment.yaml` with 3 replicas of an image, and a cluster that is healthy. You type `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` and press enter.

Between that keypress and a container serving traffic, at least nine separate pieces do their bit — and none of them tells the next one what to do. Follow it the whole way.

steps.title: Your laptop builds an HTTPS request

ask.prompt: Before anything is sent, what does `kubectl` do with your YAML?
choices: Converts it to JSON and POSTs it to the API server, authenticating with the credentials in your kubeconfig
Sends the YAML straight to the scheduler, which owns placement
Writes it into etcd over port 2379
Hands it to the kubelet on the nearest node
ask.explain: kubectl is an ordinary HTTP client. It has no special powers and no private channel — everything it does, you could do with curl and the right certificate.

steps.body:
`kubectl` reads your kubeconfig for the API server address and your credentials, converts the YAML to JSON, and sends it as an HTTP request to the API server.

That is the whole client side. There is no agent, no daemon, no queue.

code.label: the request, unmasked
code.text:
$ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -v=8
POST https://k8s-prod.internal:6443/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/prod/deployments?fieldManager=kubectl
Request Headers:
    Authorization: Bearer <redacted>
    Content-Type: application/json
Response Status: 201 Created in 31 milliseconds

steps.watch: `-v=8` on any kubectl command shows you the raw HTTP. It is the fastest way to see that nothing else is going on.

steps.title: The gate: authentication, authorization, admission

ask.prompt: A mutating webhook injects a sidecar, and a policy engine requires every container to have memory limits. In what order does the API server run them?
choices: Mutating first, then validating — so the injected sidecar is also checked by the policy
Validating first, so the sidecar is never subject to policy
Both at once, and the API server merges the results
Whichever webhook registered first
ask.explain: Mutating always precedes validating. That ordering is deliberate: it means nothing can be injected into an object *after* the checks have run. It is also why an injected sidecar with no memory limit gets your whole Deployment rejected.

steps.body:
The request walks a fixed pipeline: **authentication** (who are you — a 401 if it fails), **authorization** (are you allowed — a 403 if it fails), **mutating admission** (defaults get filled in, sidecars get injected), **schema validation**, then **validating admission** (quota, policy, your own webhooks).

Only after all of that is the object written to etcd, given a `resourceVersion`, and returned to you as `201 Created`.

When you read an error, its shape tells you how far you got: 401 never reached RBAC, 403 passed authentication, and a message naming a webhook means you passed everything before admission.

code.label: the object exists now — but nothing is running
code.text:
$ kubectl get deploy api
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
api    0/3     0            0           1s

$ kubectl get pods -l app=api
No resources found in prod namespace.
code.note: This gap is the whole point: apply only records intent. Everything after this is other components noticing.

steps.title: A controller notices, and makes a ReplicaSet

ask.prompt: How does the deployment controller find out that your Deployment exists?
choices: It has an open watch on Deployments and receives the change as an event, then reconciles from its cache
The API server calls it over gRPC and hands it the object
It polls etcd every 30 seconds
kubectl notifies it after the write succeeds
ask.explain: Every controller in Kubernetes is built the same way: watch, cache, reconcile. Nothing pushes work to a controller, which is why a controller can crash, restart, and simply pick up where the world is now.

steps.body:
The deployment controller — one of dozens of loops inside kube-controller-manager — has a watch open on Deployments. Your write arrives as an event, it looks at the current state of the object, and sees: 3 replicas wanted, 0 exist.

So it creates a **ReplicaSet**, named with a hash of the pod template, with an `ownerReference` pointing back at the Deployment.

Then it stops. It does not create pods — that is a different controller's job.

code.label: one object created another
code.text:
$ kubectl get rs -l app=api
NAME              DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
api-6b8f9c7d4d    3         3         0       2s

$ kubectl get rs api-6b8f9c7d4d -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0]}'
{"apiVersion":"apps/v1","kind":"Deployment","name":"api","uid":"3f2b...","controller":true}
code.note: That ownerReference is how the garbage collector will clean up later. It matches on uid, not name.

steps.title: Three pod objects appear — with no node
steps.body:
A second controller watches ReplicaSets. It sees one wanting 3 pods and counting 0, so it creates three Pod objects, each owned by the ReplicaSet.

These pods are real API objects now, but they are **Pending** and their `spec.nodeName` is empty. No node knows about them. No container exists anywhere.

code.label: pods exist, nowhere
code.text:
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api -o wide
NAME                   READY   STATUS    NODE     AGE
api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p   0/1     Pending   <none>   1s
api-6b8f9c7d4d-7w4mz   0/1     Pending   <none>   1s
api-6b8f9c7d4d-p9c3v   0/1     Pending   <none>   1s

steps.watch: If a pod stays like this, the problem is scheduling — resources, taints, affinity or an unbound volume. `kubectl describe pod` will name the reason on every node it rejected.

steps.title: Filter, score, and write one field

ask.prompt: The scheduler picks node2. What does it physically do next?
choices: Writes a Binding to the API server, which sets the pod's spec.nodeName to node2
Opens a connection to node2's kubelet and sends it the pod spec
Asks containerd on node2 to pull the image
Updates the ReplicaSet with the chosen node
ask.explain: The scheduler fills in one field and stops. It never talks to a node. This is why you can bypass it entirely by setting `nodeName` yourself — and why doing so skips every resource and taint check it would have done.

steps.body:
The scheduler watches for pods with an empty `nodeName`. For each one it runs two phases:

- **Filter** — which nodes could run this? Enough unbooked CPU and memory, taints tolerated, node selectors and affinity satisfied, volumes reachable from that zone.
- **Score** — of the survivors, which is best? Spread across zones, least-booked resources, image already cached locally.

It writes a Binding, and its involvement ends. Note it scores on **requests**, not on real usage: a node at 95% actual CPU with small requests booked still looks roomy.

code.label: one field, and the world moves
code.text:
$ kubectl get pod api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'
node2

$ kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p
TYPE     REASON      MESSAGE
Normal   Scheduled   Successfully assigned prod/api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p to node2

steps.title: The node picks up its own work

ask.prompt: How does node2's kubelet learn it has a pod to run?
choices: It is watching the API server for pods whose spec.nodeName matches its own node name
The scheduler pushed the assignment to it
kube-proxy relayed it from the control plane
It polls the ReplicaSet controller
ask.explain: Nothing in the control plane ever initiates a connection to a node to hand out work. Nodes pull. That is why a node behind NAT works fine, and why a node that was offline catches up on its own when it comes back.

steps.body:
The kubelet on node2 has been watching for pods bound to `node2` all along. Yours appears, and it starts building it.

First it needs a place to put the containers: it calls containerd over the **CRI** socket to create a **pod sandbox** — the `pause` container that will own the network namespace.

code.label: on the node itself, no kubectl needed
code.text:
$ export CONTAINER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT=unix:///run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock
$ crictl pods --name api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p
POD ID         NAME                   STATE       NAMESPACE
a1b2c3d4e5f6   api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p   SANDBOX_READY  prod
code.note: On RKE2 that socket path is the k3s one — RKE2 runs its own bundled containerd, not the host's.

steps.title: The pod gets an IP
steps.body:
With the sandbox created, the kubelet invokes the **CNI** plugin — Canal by default on RKE2. It allocates an IP from this node's slice of the cluster CIDR and wires the namespace to the node's network.

Until this succeeds the pod sits in `ContainerCreating`. On a freshly joined node this is the classic chicken-and-egg: the CNI itself runs as a pod, so the node is NotReady until that DaemonSet lands.

code.label: each node owns a slice of the pod network
code.text:
$ kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDR:.spec.podCIDR
node1   10.42.0.0/24
node2   10.42.1.0/24
node3   10.42.2.0/24

$ kubectl get pod api-6b8f9c7d4d-2xk9p -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}'
10.42.1.37

steps.title: The image is pulled and the process starts

ask.prompt: The image pull fails with an x509 error against your internal registry, on every node. Where is the fix?
choices: /etc/rancher/rke2/registries.yaml, then restart rke2-server/rke2-agent
An imagePullSecret in the namespace
The Deployment's securityContext
The kubelet's --node-ip flag
ask.explain: Pulling images is containerd's job, not Kubernetes'. imagePullSecrets solve authentication per namespace; registry TLS trust and mirrors are node-level containerd config, which RKE2 renders from registries.yaml at startup.

steps.body:
containerd pulls the image (if it is not cached), unpacks it, and starts a shim. The shim calls **runc**, which creates the namespaces and cgroups and finally execs your process.

The cgroup limits come straight from your manifest: `limits.memory` becomes a hard ceiling the kernel enforces with a kill, and `limits.cpu` becomes a quota the kernel enforces by throttling.

code.label: the whole chain
code.text:
kubelet -> CRI (gRPC) -> containerd -> containerd-shim -> runc -> your process

failures map cleanly onto it:
  ErrImagePull / registry x509   -> containerd
  permission or cgroup errors    -> runc
  context deadline on the socket -> kubelet <-> containerd

steps.title: Readiness turns the pod into a backend

ask.prompt: The container is running but its readiness probe is failing. What is true?
choices: The pod stays out of the Service's EndpointSlice, so it receives no traffic — and it is not restarted
The kubelet restarts the container until readiness passes
The pod is evicted and rescheduled elsewhere
It receives traffic anyway; readiness is only reported in kubectl
ask.explain: Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts. Mixing them up is the single most expensive probe mistake — a liveness probe that checks your database turns a dependency blip into a cluster-wide restart storm.

steps.body:
The kubelet starts running probes and reports status back to the API server. Once the readiness probe passes, the pod is marked Ready.

The **endpointslice controller** is watching for exactly that: it adds the pod's IP to the Service's EndpointSlice. **kube-proxy** on every node sees the EndpointSlice change and rewrites the kernel rules so the Service's ClusterIP can now land on this pod.

Only now does traffic reach your container.

code.label: the last link in the chain
code.text:
$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
NAME        ADDRESSTYPE   ENDPOINTS                            PORTS
api-x7k2p   IPv4          10.42.1.37,10.42.2.9,10.42.0.14      8080

$ kubectl get deploy api
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
api    3/3     3            3           24s

steps.watch: A Service that returns connection refused almost always has an empty EndpointSlice — either the selector matches nothing, or nothing is Ready.

takeaways: `apply` only records intent. Everything after it is independent components noticing and reacting.
Nobody pushes work to a node. The kubelet pulls the pods assigned to it, which is why nodes recover on their own.
Each hop has its own failure signature: Pending is the scheduler, ContainerCreating is the kubelet's setup, CrashLoopBackOff is your app.
Readiness is the switch that puts a pod into a Service. Liveness is the switch that restarts it.
